content: The HAM1 gene in the yeast species Saccharomyces cerevisiae has been found to produce two distinct transcript variants, each encoding a different isoform of the protein. Additionally, at least two other transcript variants have been identified, which are believed to serve regulatory functions rather than encoding proteins. The protein encoded by this gene functions as an enzyme that hydrolyzes inosine triphosphate (ITP) and deoxyinosine triphosphate (dITP) into their respective monophosphate nucleotides and diphosphate byproducts. This enzyme exhibits broad substrate specificity, meaning it can also act on other nucleotide substrates, such as xanthosine triphosphate (XTP) and deoxyxanthosine triphosphate (dXTP). The protein belongs to the HAM1 NTPase family and is localized in the cytoplasm, where it functions as a homodimer. Clinically, defects in the protein encoded by this gene can lead to a condition known as inosine triphosphate pyrophosphorylase deficiency.
